claim: Vertebrate and invertebrate hearts require stereotyped arrangements of diverse cell populations for coordinated circulation.
source: For coordinated circulation, vertebrate and invertebrate hearts require stereotyped arrangements of diverse cell populations.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about heart structure and function.

claim: The Drosophila heart contains two major cardioblast subpopulations: generic working myocardial cells and inflow valve-forming ostial cardioblasts.
source: This study explores the process of cardiac cell diversification in the Drosophila heart, focusing on the two major cardioblast subpopulations: generic working myocardial cells and inflow valve-forming ostial cardioblasts.
evidence: This is a direct statement from the abstract describing the focus of the study, supported by established knowledge of Drosophila heart structure.

claim: EGF signaling is specifically required for the specification of generic cardioblasts and a subset of pericardial cells.
source: Further analysis revealed an unexpected, specific requirement of EGF signaling for the specification of generic cardioblasts and a subset of pericardial cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including mutant analysis and immunostaining results shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: The Tbx20 ortholog Midline acts as a direct target of the EGFR effector Pointed to repress ostial fates.
source: We demonstrate that the Tbx20 ortholog Midline acts as a direct target of the EGFR effector Pointed to repress ostial fates.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data including enhancer analysis (Figure 9) and genetic epistasis experiments (Figure 7).

claim: Edl/Mae is an antagonist of the ETS factor Pointed.
source: Furthermore, we identified Edl/Mae, an antagonist of the ETS factor Pointed, as a novel cardiac regulator crucial for ostial cardioblast specification.
evidence: This is supported by both citation to previous work and experimental data in this study showing genetic interactions between edl and pnt.

claim: Edl/Mae is crucial for ostial cardioblast specification.
source: Furthermore, we identified Edl/Mae, an antagonist of the ETS factor Pointed, as a novel cardiac regulator crucial for ostial cardioblast specification.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing loss of ostial cardioblasts in edl mutants (Figure 4).

claim: The balance between activation of Pointed and its inhibition by Edl controls cardioblast subtype-specific gene expression.
source: Combining these findings, we propose a regulatory model in which the balance between activation of Pointed and its inhibition by Edl controls cardioblast subtype-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the integration of multiple experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The vertebrate T-box gene Tbx20 promotes working myocardial fate by restricting Tbx2 expression and enabling the expression of chamber myocardium-specific genes.
source: For example, the vertebrate T-box gene Tbx20 promotes working myocardial fate by restricting Tbx2 expression and enabling the expression of chamber myocardium-specific genes (Cai et al., 2005; Singh et al., 2005; Stennard et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tbx2 and Tbx3 repress working myocardium-specific gene expression and chamber differentiation in the non-chamber myocardium.
source: By contrast, Tbx2 and Tbx3 repress working myocardium-specific gene expression and chamber differentiation in the non-chamber myocardium and thus contribute to the formation of endocardial cushions and structures of the conduction system (Christoffels et al., 2004; Hoogaars et al., 2007; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Normal endocardial cushion formation requires COUP-TFII.
source: Normal endocardial cushion formation also requires COUP-TFII, an orphan nuclear receptor transcription factor that regulates cell fate decisions in several tissues (Lin et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the embryonic mouse myocardium, COUP-TFII is restricted to atrial cardiomyocytes.
source: In the embryonic mouse myocardium, COUP-TFII is restricted to atrial cardiomyocytes, a pattern consistent with a fate determination function that confers atrial over ventricular fate (Lin et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: COUP-TFII function in conferring atrial over ventricular fate appears to involve the up-regulation of Tbx5.
source: This function appears to involve the up-regulation of Tbx5 (Wu et al., 2013), another T-box gene with non-uniform cardiac expression and a fundamental role in heart development and human cardiac disease (Basson et al., 1997; Bruneau et al., 1999; Bruneau et al., 2001; Ghosh et al., 2017; Steimle and Moskowitz, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FGF-mediated receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling upstream of Nkx2-5 is required for the maintenance of ventricular chamber identity of cardiomyocytes in zebrafish.
source: Furthermore, FGF-mediated receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) signaling upstream of the cardiogenic transcription factor Nkx2-5 was recently shown to be required for the maintenance of ventricular chamber identity of cardiomyocytes in zebrafish (Pradhan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Spatial restriction of cardiac transcription factors is important in both vertebrate and invertebrate hearts.
source: As emphasized below, spatial restriction of cardiac transcription factors as well as precisely controlled RTK signaling activities are not only important in vertebrate but also invertebrate hearts (Gajewski et al., 2000; Lo and Frasch, 2001; Zaffran et al., 2006; this work).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and data from the current work.

claim: The Drosophila heart (dorsal vessel) comprises several types of cardiomyocytes and non-contractile pericardial cells.
source: The Drosophila heart (dorsal vessel) comprises several types of cardiomyocytes (in the embryo called cardioblasts, CBs) and non-contractile pericardial cells (PCs) (Bodmer and Frasch, 2010; Lovato and Cripps, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The progenitors of Drosophila heart cells are specified in segmentally repeated heart fields located at the intersection of BMP/Dpp and Wg/Wnt signaling activities.
source: The progenitors of these cells are specified in segmentally repeated heart fields located at the intersection of BMP/Dpp and Wg/Wnt signaling activities (Frasch, 1995; Reim and Frasch, 2005; Wu et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specification of the definitive cardiogenic mesoderm depends on tinman, pannier, and Dorsocross1-3 T-box genes.
source: Subsequent specification of the definitive cardiogenic mesoderm depends on a conserved group of transcription factors, most importantly those encoded by the Nkx2-5 ortholog tinman (tin), the Gata4 ortholog pannier (pnr) and the Dorsocross1-3 T-box genes (three Tbx6-related paralogs that also share features with Tbx2/3/5; in the following collectively called Doc) (Alvarez et al., 2003; Azpiazu and Frasch, 1993; Bodmer, 1993; Gajewski et al., 1999; Junion et al., 2012; Reim and Frasch, 2005; Reim et al., 2003; reviewed in Reim and Frasch, 2010; Reim et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Generic cardioblasts (gCBs) build the main portion of the contractile tube ('working myocardium').
source: In this study, we mainly focus on the development of the two major cardioblast subpopulations: generic cardioblasts (gCBs), which build the main portion of the contractile tube ('working myocardium'), and ostial cardioblasts (oCBs), which form bi-cellular valves (ostia) for hemolymph inflow.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila heart structure.

claim: Ostial cardioblasts (oCBs) form bi-cellular valves (ostia) for hemolymph inflow.
source: In this study, we mainly focus on the development of the two major cardioblast subpopulations: generic cardioblasts (gCBs), which build the main portion of the contractile tube ('working myocardium'), and ostial cardioblasts (oCBs), which form bi-cellular valves (ostia) for hemolymph inflow.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about Drosophila heart structure.

claim: Ostial progenitor specification is limited to the abdominal region due to Hox gene inputs.
source: Due to Hox gene inputs, ostial progenitor specification is limited to the abdominal region (Lo et al., 2002; Lovato et al., 2002; Ponzielli et al., 2002; Ryan et al., 2005; reviewed in Monier et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Each abdominal hemisegment generates at least seven distinct progenitors that give rise to six CBs (4 gCBs + 2 oCBs) and several types of PCs.
source: Current research suggests that each abdominal hemisegment generates at least seven distinct progenitors that give rise to six CBs (4 gCBs + 2 oCBs) and several types of PCs (Tin+/Even-skipped[Eve]+ EPCs, Tin+ TPCs, and Odd-skipped[Odd]+ OPCs; Bodmer and Frasch, 2010 and references therein).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Generic cardioblasts (gCBs) maintain expression of tinman.
source: Whereas gCBs (a.k.a. Tin-CBs) maintain expression of tin, oCBs (a.k.a. Svp-CBs) specifically express the COUP-TFII ortholog seven-up (svp) and Doc (Gajewski et al., 2000; Lo and Frasch, 2001; Ward and Skeath, 2000; Zaffran et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ostial cardioblasts (oCBs) specifically express seven-up (svp) and Doc.
source: Whereas gCBs (a.k.a. Tin-CBs) maintain expression of tin, oCBs (a.k.a. Svp-CBs) specifically express the COUP-TFII ortholog seven-up (svp) and Doc (Gajewski et al., 2000; Lo and Frasch, 2001; Ward and Skeath, 2000; Zaffran et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Doc is repressed in gCBs in a tin-dependent manner.
source: Previous work has shown that Doc is repressed in gCBs in a tin-dependent manner (Zaffran et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Robust tin expression in gCBs depends on the Tbx20 ortholog midline (mid/nmr2).
source: Robust tin expression in turn depends on the Tbx20 ortholog midline (mid/nmr2).
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work cited in the manuscript.

claim: The mid gene is first activated in gCB progenitors, but later becomes expressed in all cardioblasts.
source: The mid gene is first activated in gCB progenitors, but later, like its paralog H15/nmr1, becomes expressed in all cardioblasts (Miskolczi-McCallum et al., 2005; Qian et al., 2005; Reim et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In oCBs, svp represses tin expression thereby permitting continued Doc expression in these cells.
source: In oCBs, svp represses tin expression thereby permitting continued Doc expression in these cells (Gajewski et al., 2000; Lo and Frasch, 2001; Zaffran et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the abdomen, gCBs and most PCs are preceded by a precursor that undergoes symmetric division.
source: In the abdomen, gCBs and most PCs are preceded by a precursor that undergoes symmetric division, whereas oCBs and half of the OPCs are derived from common, asymmetrically dividing CB/PC progenitors (Alvarez et al., 2003; Han and Bodmer, 2003; Ward and Skeath, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: oCBs and half of the OPCs are derived from common, asymmetrically dividing CB/PC progenitors.
source: In the abdomen, gCBs and most PCs are preceded by a precursor that undergoes symmetric division, whereas oCBs and half of the OPCs are derived from common, asymmetrically dividing CB/PC progenitors (Alvarez et al., 2003; Han and Bodmer, 2003; Ward and Skeath, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The process of progenitor specification in the somatic and cardiogenic mesoderm involves the antagonistic actions of RTK/Ras/MAPK and Delta/Notch signaling.
source: The process of progenitor specification in the somatic and cardiogenic mesoderm involves the antagonistic actions of RTK/Ras/MAPK and Delta/Notch signaling (Carmena et al., 2002; Grigorian et al., 2011; Hartenstein et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two types of RTKs, the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor Heartless (Htl) and the epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor EGFR, act positively on progenitor selection via MAPK signaling.
source: Two types of RTKs, the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor Heartless (Htl) and the epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor EGFR, act positively on progenitor selection via MAPK signaling, although they are used by different progenitors to different extents (Buff et al., 1998; Carmena et al., 2002; Michelson et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Htl and its FGF8-like ligands Pyramus (Pyr) and Thisbe (Ths) have a dual function as regulators of mesodermal cell migration and cell specification.
source: Htl and its FGF8-like ligands Pyramus (Pyr) and Thisbe (Ths) have a dual function as regulators of mesodermal cell migration and cell specification, with progenitors of the Eve+ lineage as the most prominent example for the latter (reviewed in Bae et al., 2012; Muha and Müller, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: EGFR signaling is dispensable for early mesoderm migration events.
source: EGFR signaling appears to be dispensable for early mesoderm migration events (Wilson et al., 2005) but has been reported to contribute to the specification of particular cell types within the mesoderm, including subsets of adult muscle precursors (AMPs; Figeac et al., 2010) and the Eve+ DA1 muscles (derived from the so-called P15 progenitors in the dorsal mesoderm; Buff et al., 1998; Carmena et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: EGFR signaling contributes to the specification of subsets of adult muscle precursors (AMPs).
source: EGFR signaling appears to be dispensable for early mesoderm migration events (Wilson et al., 2005) but has been reported to contribute to the specification of particular cell types within the mesoderm, including subsets of adult muscle precursors (AMPs; Figeac et al., 2010) and the Eve+ DA1 muscles (derived from the so-called P15 progenitors in the dorsal mesoderm; Buff et al., 1998; Carmena et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Eve+ pericardial cells derived from the P2 progenitor form independent of EGFR activity.
source: By contrast, Eve+pericardial cells derived from the P2 progenitor were shown to form independent of EGFR activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: EGFR loss-of-function results in a severe reduction of the numbers of cardioblasts, pericardial nephrocytes, and blood progenitors.
source: The exact contribution of EGFR signaling to Drosophila heart development has been less clear until now, but it was shown that EGFR loss-of-function results in a severe reduction of the numbers of cardioblasts, pericardial nephrocytes, and blood progenitors (Grigorian et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The predominant EGFR ligand in the embryo, Spitz (Spi), relies on the protease Rhomboid (encoded by rho) and the chaperon Star (S) for its conversion from a membrane-bound into its active form.
source: Molecularly, the predominant EGFR ligand in the embryo, Spitz (Spi), relies on the protease Rhomboid (encoded by rho) and the chaperon Star (S) for its conversion from a membrane-bound into its active form (reviewed in Shilo, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: rho expression is restricted to a limited number of cells in a complex and dynamic pattern, including cells of the cardiogenic area.
source: In contrast to spi, rho expression is restricted to a limited number of cells in a complex and dynamic pattern, including cells of the cardiogenic area (Bidet et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2006), which points to rho expression being the most decisive factor for Spi-mediated EGFR activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PntP2 becomes an active transcriptional activator upon phosphorylation by MAPK.
source: Among the most important downstream effectors of RTK/Ras/MAPK pathways are the ETS transcription factors PntP2 (encoded by pointed/pnt) and Yan/Aop (encoded by anterior open/aop). While PntP2 becomes an active transcriptional activator upon phosphorylation by MAPK, the transcriptional repressor Yan is negatively regulated by MAPK (Gabay et al., 1996; O'Neill et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The transcriptional repressor Yan is negatively regulated by MAPK.
source: Among the most important downstream effectors of RTK/Ras/MAPK pathways are the ETS transcription factors PntP2 (encoded by pointed/pnt) and Yan/Aop (encoded by anterior open/aop). While PntP2 becomes an active transcriptional activator upon phosphorylation by MAPK, the transcriptional repressor Yan is negatively regulated by MAPK (Gabay et al., 1996; O'Neill et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PntP1 is constitutively active but requires activated MAPK for its transcriptional activation in some cell types.
source: Unlike PntP2, a shorter isoform encoded by pnt, PntP1, is constitutively active but was shown to require activated MAPK for its transcriptional activation at least in some cell types (Brunner et al., 1994; Gabay et al., 1996; Klämbt, 1993; O'Neill et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chordate Pnt orthologs (ETS1/2) contribute to cardiac progenitor formation in the tunicate Ciona.
source: Notably, chordate Pnt orthologs (ETS1/2) were shown to contribute to cardiac progenitor formation in the tunicate Ciona and during transdifferentiation of human dermal fibroblasts into cardiac progenitors (Davidson et al., 2006; Islas et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During early Drosophila cardiogenesis, Pnt favors expression of eve over that of ladybird (lbe).
source: During early Drosophila cardiogenesis, Pnt favors expression of eve over that of another homeobox gene, ladybird (lbe, expressed in mesodermal cells immediately anterior of the Eve+ cluster and later in TPCs and two of the four gCBs per hemisegment; Jagla et al., 1997) (Liu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pnt promotes pericardial cell development and antagonizes CB fate, especially that of oCBs.
source: In addition, Pnt promotes pericardial cell development and antagonizes CB fate, especially that of oCBs (Alvarez et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: An EMS mutagenesis screen was performed to identify genes involved in heart and muscle development in Drosophila melanogaster embryos.
source: In order to identify genes involved in heart and muscle development in an unbiased manner, we have performed an EMS mutagenesis screen for chromosome two in Drosophila melanogaster embryos (Hollfelder et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Several isolated mutants display a partial loss or irregular alignment of cardioblasts.
source: Several of the isolated mutants display a partial loss or irregular alignment of cardioblasts (CBs).
evidence: This is a description of the phenotypes observed in the screen.

claim: Embryos with partially reduced FGF/Htl signaling show an about equal reduction of gCB and oCB numbers.
source: Embryos with partially reduced FGF/Htl signaling, that is mutants lacking both copies of the FGF-encoding gene pyr and one copy of its paralog ths, as well as hypomorphic htl mutants, show an about equal reduction of gCB and oCB numbers (Figure 1B, for quantification see Figure 1M; additional examples in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B, 1M, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: In strong Egfr mutants very few CBs can be found, and the overwhelming majority of the residual CBs express Doc.
source: In strong Egfr mutants very few CBs can be found (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E). Remarkably, the overwhelming majority of the residual CBs express Doc.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: In spitz, rhomboid and Star loss-of-function mutants, the number of Doc-/Tin+ CBs is strongly reduced while that of ostial Doc+/Tin- CBs is nearly normal or in some cases even increased.
source: In spitz, rhomboid and Star loss-of-function mutants, the number of Doc-/Tin+ CBs is strongly reduced while that of ostial Doc+/Tin- CBs is nearly normal or in some cases even increased by a few cells (Figure 1D–G,M, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Both Lbe+ and Lbe- gCB subtypes are about equally represented in rho mutants.
source: However, our finding that both types are about equally represented in rho mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) argues against this assumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Segment-by-segment analysis in homozygous rhoL68 mutants reveals that residual gCBs most frequently occur either as Lbe+ or Lbe- pairs.
source: Moreover, segment-by-segment analysis in homozygous rhoL68 mutants reveals that residual gCBs most frequently occur either as Lbe+ or Lbe- pairs, whereas none of the analyzed residual gCB duplets consisted of a combination of both gCB types.
evidence: This is a description of quantitative analysis of mutant phenotypes.

claim: EGF function is required for the formation of gCB progenitors prior to their final division.
source: This suggests that EGF function is required for the formation of gCB progenitors prior to their final division.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that residual gCBs occur as pairs of the same subtype.

claim: Progenitors of the oCB lineage develop and survive independently of EGF.
source: Notably, progenitors of the oCB lineage apparently do not require activity of the ostial marker gene svp to develop and survive independently of EGF, since total CB numbers are similar in Star single and Star svp double mutants (compare Figure 1H–1G; quantification in Figure 1M).
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing Star single and Star svp double mutants shown in Figure 1G, 1H, and 1M.

claim: At stage 11, rho is detectable in clusters C14/C16 of the cardiac mesoderm.
source: At stage 11, rho is detectable in clusters C14/C16 of the cardiac mesoderm (arrowheads) and is fading from the central Doc-negative region containing EPC and somatic muscle progenitors (empty arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Stage 11 rho expression is still robustly observed in all C14/C16 clusters in S mutants.
source: Of note, stage 11 rho expression is still robustly observed in all C14/C16 clusters in S mutants (Figure 2E cf. 2A), showing that earlier patterning events are not disrupted in this situation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing wild type and S mutants shown in Figure 2A and 2E.

claim: During stage 12, a reduction of rho expressing cells is apparent in S mutants.
source: Later during stage 12, when rho RNA is normally found in developing CBs along the dorsal mesoderm margin, a reduction of rho expressing cells is apparent in S mutants (Figure 2F cf. 2C), which is consistent with defects in CB progenitor formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing wild type and S mutants shown in Figure 2C and 2F.

claim: Detection of active diphospho-MAPK is severely reduced in cardiac cells of S mutants at stage 11 and during stage 12.
source: Importantly, detection of active diphospho-MAPK is severely reduced in cardiac cells of S mutants already in the cardiogenic clusters at stage 11 as well as during 12 in which dpMAPK is normally detected in both ostial and generic CB progenitors (Figure 2H,J cf. 2G,I; later activity in cardiac cells appears to be less affected; Figure 2L cf. 2K).
evidence: This claim is supported by data comparing wild type and S mutants shown in Figure 2G-L.

claim: EGF signaling serves as the major positive input for MAPK activation during early gCB progenitor formation.
source: Altogether, this demonstrates that EGF signaling serves as the major positive input for MAPK activation during early gCB progenitor formation, whereas input from FGFs may gain importance in developing CBs at later stages for CB fate maintenance as was proposed previously (Grigorian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dpMAPK staining data and previous work.

claim: The timing of EGF signals is crucial for their function in differential progenitor specification.
source: Our overexpression studies demonstrate that the timing of EGF signals is crucial for their function in differential progenitor specification.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the overexpression experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Early pan-mesodermal activation of MAPK signaling or expression of constitutive active Pnt forms via the twi-GAL4 driver reduces the numbers of all cardiac cells except the Eve+ progenitors.
source: While early pan-mesodermal activation of MAPK signaling or expression of constitutive active Pnt forms via the twi-GAL4 driver reduces the numbers of all cardiac cells except the Eve+ progenitors (Alvarez et al., 2003; Bidet et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2006; and our own data), later MAPK activation favors formation of the symmetrically dividing OPC, TPC and gCB progenitor subpopulations (e.g. as seen in our experiments with tinD-GAL4-driven rho).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and data from the current work.

claim: Later MAPK activation favors formation of the symmetrically dividing OPC, TPC and gCB progenitor subpopulations.
source: While early pan-mesodermal activation of MAPK signaling or expression of constitutive active Pnt forms via the twi-GAL4 driver reduces the numbers of all cardiac cells except the Eve+ progenitors (Alvarez et al., 2003; Bidet et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2006; and our own data), later MAPK activation favors formation of the symmetrically dividing OPC, TPC and gCB progenitor subpopulations (e.g. as seen in our experiments with tinD-GAL4-driven rho).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from the current work.

claim: Cardioblast formation as such is independent of pnt.
source: As discussed above, cardioblast formation as such is independent of pnt.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that pnt mutants have increased CB numbers.

claim: MAPK activity in the context of CB progenitor selection might be primarily required to eliminate the repressive activity of Yan.
source: How could this be achieved? Growth factor-activated MAPK can also phosphorylate the repressor Yan thereby diminishing its activity as an antagonist of progenitor selection (Halfon et al., 2000; O'Neill et al., 1994; Rebay and Rubin, 1995). Therefore, it is conceivable that MAPK activity in the context of CB progenitor selection might be primarily required to eliminate the repressive activity of Yan.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on known functions of MAPK and Yan.

claim: mid is a key target gene of Pnt in gCB progenitors.
source: We identified mid as a key target gene of Pnt in gCB progenitors based on its early gCB-specific expression, Pnt-dependent transcriptional regulation and its ability to repress the oCB-specific regulator gene svp.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including expression analysis, genetic epistasis, and enhancer analysis.

claim: svp suppression by Mid provides an important part of the explanation for the positive role of Mid in maintaining tin expression in gCBs.
source: Since Svp represses tin expression (Gajewski et al., 2000; Lo and Frasch, 2001), svp suppression provides an important part of the explanation for the previously reported positive role of Mid in maintaining tin expression in gCBs (Qian et al., 2005; Reim et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current data and previous work.

claim: Expanded expression of tin in mid svp double mutants argues against the possibility that Mid stimulates tin expression directly.
source: Furthermore, expanded expression of tin in mid svp double mutants argues against the possibility that Mid stimulates tin expression directly.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of mid svp double mutants shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Tin does not repress svp.
source: While Tin acts as a repressor of Doc via unknown mechanisms in gCBs, it does not repress svp (Zaffran et al., 2006; Figure 7—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In the early cardiogenic mesoderm, Tin acts as an activator of svp in oCB progenitors.
source: On the contrary, at least in the early cardiogenic mesoderm, it acts as an activator of svp in oCB progenitors (Ryan et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: In the absence of appropriate repressors such as Mid, svp expression can expand into gCBs.
source: Thus, in the absence of appropriate repressors such as Mid, svp expression can expand into gCBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation of svp expansion in mid mutants.

claim: Edl is required for svp and Doc gene activity in oCB progenitors.
source: Our phenotypic analysis demonstrates that Edl is required for svp and Doc gene activity (the latter being due to restriction of tin expression) as well as the restriction of PntP2-dependent PntP1 expression in cardiac progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of edl mutants shown in Figures 4, 6, and 7.

claim: Edl acts primarily by inhibiting Pnt during cardiac cell diversification.
source: The comparison of single and double mutant phenotypes, combined with the reproducibility of nearly all aspects of the cardiac pnt phenotype by Edl overexpression, implies that Edl acts primarily by inhibiting Pnt during cardiac cell diversification, although we cannot fully exclude additional interactions with Yan.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The PntP1 isoform is activated specifically in gCB progenitors in a PntP2-dependent and EGF-sensitive fashion.
source: Our model of CB diversification incorporates the observation that the PntP1 isoform is activated specifically in gCB progenitors in a PntP2-dependent and EGF-sensitive fashion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of PntP1 expression shown in Figure 7.

claim: PntP1 becomes activated at a particular threshold of MAPK/PntP2 activity.
source: We propose that PntP1 becomes activated at a particular threshold of MAPK/PntP2 activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed pattern of PntP1 expression.

claim: The activation of PntP1 marks a point of no return for CB diversification, because PntP1 cannot be inhibited via Edl.
source: This activation marks a point of no return for CB diversification, because PntP1 cannot be inhibited via Edl.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the known molecular properties of PntP1 and Edl.

claim: mid is a direct and functionally critical target of Pnt during cardiac cell diversification.
source: Although the exact details of this activation as well as the direct binding of Pnt to particular sites in vivo remain to be investigated, the sum of our genetic and enhancer data provide strong indications for mid being a direct and functionally critical target of Pnt during cardiac cell diversification.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including enhancer analysis and genetic epistasis.

claim: The timing of Mid protein appearance is linked to its capability to interfere with svp expression.
source: Thus, by regulating Pnt activity, the timing of Mid protein appearance can be controlled. We predict that this timing is linked to its capability to interfere with svp expression, since later presence of Mid in all CB subtypes including oCBs (mediated by other, Pnt-independent mechanisms; see Figure 9F,H,J) does not lead to svp repression.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observation that Mid is present in oCBs at later stages without repressing svp.

claim: Many of the CEE-containing Tin target enhancers might also be targets of Pnt or Yan.
source: Thus, many of the CEE-containing Tin target enhancers might in fact also be targets of Pnt (potentially mediating ETS-dependent activation) or Yan (potentially mediating ETS-dependent repression in the absence of MAPK signals).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the similarity between CEE motifs and ETS binding sites.

claim: A combination of closely spaced Tin and ETS binding sites might be a key signature in enhancers of working myocardial genes.
source: Therefore, a combination of closely spaced Tin and ETS binding sites might be a key signature in enhancers of working myocardial genes, although additional features must be present in their architecture to distinguish them from Tin+ETS binding site-containing enhancers active in pericardial cells or their progenitors (Halfon et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the analysis of the mid enhancer and previous work.

claim: Pnt proteins might stimulate Delta transcription in gCBs to control OPC development in a non-autonomous manner.
source: Hence, it is conceivable that Pnt proteins might stimulate Delta transcription in gCBs to control OPC development in a non-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known upregulation of Delta by MAPK activity.

claim: pnt mutants feature an extreme bias in the increase of oCBs that has not been observed in Notch pathway mutants.
source: However, because of the herein described function of Pnt in suppressing svp transcription and oCB fate, pnt mutants feature an extreme bias in the increase of oCBs that has not been observed in Notch pathway mutants (Albrecht et al., 2006; this work).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of pnt and Notch pathway mutant phenotypes.

claim: Factors that tilt the balance between PntP2 activity and Edl will have a major impact on CB subtype choice.
source: Our model proposes that factors which tilt the balance between PntP2 activity and Edl will have a major impact on CB subtype choice (see Figure 10).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the regulatory model proposed in the manuscript.

claim: Any input that modestly increases MAPK/PntP2 activity within the appropriate window of time would favor gCB fate.
source: Thus, any input that modestly increases MAPK/PntP2 activity within the appropriate window of time would favor gCB fate, whereas factors that have the opposite effect should promote oCB specification.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed regulatory model.

claim: A prime candidate for an instructive cue to anterior-posterior positioning within each segment could be Hh.
source: A prime candidate for an instructive cue to anterior-posterior positioning within each segment could be Hh (indicated in the extended model in Figure 10—figure supplement 1), because it was proposed to be an oCB-promoting and rho/MAPK pathway-modulating signal towards the cardiogenic mesoderm in previous studies (Liu et al., 2006; Ponzielli et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous studies.

claim: Observed persistent edl expression in Notch pathway mutants argues against positive inputs from Notch during edl regulation in oCB progenitors.
source: However, observed persistent edl expression in Notch pathway mutants argues against positive inputs from Notch during edl regulation in oCB progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of edl expression in Notch pathway mutants shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A SAM domain-only isoform of the human Yan-relative TEL2 as well as Drosophila Edl can inhibit transcriptional stimulation by the mammalian Pnt orthologs ETS1/ETS2 in cell culture.
source: Although no clear ortholog of Edl appears to be present in vertebrates, a SAM domain-only isoform of the human Yan-relative TEL2 as well as Drosophila Edl were shown to inhibit transcriptional stimulation by the mammalian Pnt orthologs ETS1/ETS2 in cell culture (Gu et al., 2001; Vivekanand and Rebay, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The restriction of ETS protein activities by protein-protein interactions offers a mechanism to fine-tune MAPK signaling output in developing tissues of both invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: Hence, the restriction of ETS protein activities by protein-protein interactions offers an intriguing mechanism to fine-tune MAPK signaling output in developing tissues of both invertebrates and vertebrates.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the findings of the study and previous work.

claim: The number of EPCs is not affected by altered levels of EGF signaling.
source: The number of EPCs is not affected by altered levels of EGF signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantification shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The number of oCB-sibling OPCs is not significantly reduced in Star mutants compared to the wild type.
source: Notably, the number of oCB-sibling OPCs (as identified by svp-lacZ reporter analysis) is not significantly reduced in Star mutants if compared to the wild type (Figure 3F,G), thus implying that the EGF signaling-dependent OPCs are those derived from symmetrically dividing OPC progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis shown in Figure 3F and 3G.

claim: The EGF signaling-dependent OPCs are those derived from symmetrically dividing OPC progenitors.
source: Notably, the number of oCB-sibling OPCs (as identified by svp-lacZ reporter analysis) is not significantly reduced in Star mutants if compared to the wild type (Figure 3F,G), thus implying that the EGF signaling-dependent OPCs are those derived from symmetrically dividing OPC progenitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that oCB-sibling OPCs are not reduced in Star mutants.

claim: EGF pathway activity is required in the mesoderm specifically for the specification of the symmetrically dividing gCB and OPCs progenitors.
source: In sum, these data demonstrate that EGF pathway activity is required in the mesoderm specifically for the specification of the symmetrically dividing gCB and OPCs progenitors (and probably also for those of the TPCs, which we did not quantify in detail) but is largely dispensable or even detrimental for the specification of the svp-expressing oCB/OPC progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of various mutants and overexpression experiments.

claim: EGF pathway activity is largely dispensable or even detrimental for the specification of the svp-expressing oCB/OPC progenitors.
source: In sum, these data demonstrate that EGF pathway activity is required in the mesoderm specifically for the specification of the symmetrically dividing gCB and OPCs progenitors (and probably also for those of the TPCs, which we did not quantify in detail) but is largely dispensable or even detrimental for the specification of the svp-expressing oCB/OPC progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of various mutants and overexpression experiments.

claim: One complementation group consisting of three alleles was mapped to the numb gene.
source: One such complementation group consisting of three alleles was mapped to the numb gene (alleles listed in Supplementary file 1-Table S1), which is consistent with its well-known function as a Notch suppressor during asymmetric cell division in the oCB lineage (Gajewski et al., 2000; Ward and Skeath, 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic mapping results.

claim: The cardiac phenotype of mutant line S0520 was caused by loss of the gene ETS domain lacking (edl) as part of a multi-gene deletion.
source: We found that its cardiac phenotype was caused by loss of the gene ETS domain lacking (edl) as part of a multi-gene deletion and named this mutant Df(2R)edl-S0520 (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2-Table S2).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic mapping results shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2-Table S2.

claim: The lacZ enhancer trap insertion allele edlk06602 has a cardiac phenotype indistinguishable from that of Df(2R)edl-S0520 and Df(2R)edl-L19.
source: The lacZ enhancer trap insertion allele edlk06602 was used in most edl loss-of-function experiments since its cardiac phenotype is indistinguishable from that of Df(2R)edl-S0520 and Df(2R)edl-L19 (Figure 4C,D and data not shown), and we detected in this strain a small deletion that specifically destroys the edl gene (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 2-Table S2).
evidence: This is a description of the characterization of the edlk06602 allele.

claim: The cardiac phenotype of edl was rescued by introducing a genomic edl transgene.
source: Furthermore, we were able to rescue the cardiac phenotype of edl by introducing a genomic edl transgene (Yamada et al., 2003; Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a description of the rescue experiment shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Phenotypic rescue of edl was achieved by artificially expressing edl in the dorsal mesoderm cells or in cardioblasts.
source: Phenotypic rescue was also achieved, albeit with lesser efficiency, by artificially expressing edl in the dorsal mesoderm cells or in cardioblasts using the drivers tinD-GAL4 and tinCΔ4-GAL4, respectively (Figure 4F,G), demonstrating that Edl is required directly within these cell types.
evidence: This is a description of the rescue experiments shown in Figure 4F and 4G.

claim: edl mRNA is found within the cardiogenic region during stages 10 to 12.
source: In accordance, edl mRNA is found within the cardiogenic region during stages 10 to 12 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D), including prominent expression in early svp-expressing oCB progenitors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is a description of the expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: After stage 12, edl expression shifts to the pericardial region, where it persists until stage 15.
source: Thereafter edl expression shifts to the pericardial region, where it persists until stage 15 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D and data not shown).
evidence: This is a description of the expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A distinctive feature of edl mutants is that the normal '2 + 4' pattern of 2 Doc+ CBs + 4 Doc- CBs is often transformed into a '1 + 5' pattern.
source: A distinctive feature of edl mutants is that the normal '2 + 4' pattern of 2 Doc+ CBs + 4 Doc- CBs is often transformed into a '1 + 5' pattern (e.g. bracket in Figure 4D), indicating a fate switch from ostial to generic CBs.
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Edl is not a direct activator of Doc expression.
source: However, Edl is not a direct activator of Doc expression because Doc is found in CBs of edl double mutants with CB-specific ablation of tin (Figure 4I), a phenotype reminiscent of that of CB-specific tin single mutants (Figure 4H; Zaffran et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of edl tin double mutants shown in Figure 4H and 4I.

claim: edl normally contributes to the activation of Doc in oCBs via suppression of tin.
source: This suggests that edl normally contributes to the activation of Doc in oCBs via suppression of tin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of edl tin double mutants.

claim: Some CBs with low levels of both Tin and Doc are observed in edl mutants.
source: This role of edl in CB patterning is further supported by the observation of some CBs with low levels of both Tin and Doc in edl mutants (Figure 4K; compare to the strictly complementary distribution of Doc and Tin in the wild type, Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Overexpressing edl in the dorsal ectoderm via pnrMD237-GAL4 has no significant effect on cardiogenesis.
source: Consistent with a mesoderm-autonomous function, overexpressing edl in the dorsal ectoderm via pnrMD237-GAL4 has no significant effect on cardiogenesis (data not shown).
evidence: This is a description of an overexpression experiment.

claim: Overexpression of edl in the entire mesoderm via twist-GAL4 results in an increase of CB numbers and a decrease of OPCs.
source: By contrast, overexpression of edl in the entire mesoderm via twist-GAL4 results in an increase of CB numbers (Figure 5A) and a decrease of OPCs (described in the next subsection).
evidence: This is a description of the overexpression phenotype shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The increase in Doc+ CBs upon edl overexpression is disproportionately high.
source: The increase in Doc+ CBs is disproportionately high.
evidence: This is a description of the quantification of the edl overexpression phenotype.

claim: The extra Doc+ CBs in the heart proper upon edl overexpression also activate ostial cell differentiation markers such as wg.
source: The extra Doc+ CBs in the heart proper also activate ostial cell differentiation markers such as wg (data not shown).
evidence: This is a description of additional characterization of the edl overexpression phenotype.

claim: The overexpression phenotypes of edl are very reminiscent to that of pntP2-specific mutants.
source: In agreement with the proposed function of Edl as a negative regulator of PntP2 (Yamada et al., 2003), our overexpression phenotypes of edl are very reminiscent to that of pntP2-specific mutants (pntRR112 reported in Alvarez et al. (2003); and pntMI03880 shown in Figure 5B) and amorphic pnt mutants (pntΔ88, pnt2; see Figure 5E,I and Alvarez et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison of phenotypes supported by data shown in Figure 5B, 5E, and 5I.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively active PntP2VP16 or PntP1 via tinD +tinCΔ4-GAL4 causes a phenotype similar to that of edl loss-of-function mutants.
source: Accordingly, overexpression of constitutively active PntP2VP16 (Figure 5C) or PntP1 (not shown) via tinD +tinCΔ4-GAL4 causes a phenotype similar to that of edl loss-of-function mutants (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is a description of the overexpression phenotype shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Overexpression of Yan/Aop leads to a loss of heart cells irrespective of their subtype.
source: By contrast, analogous overexpression of the potential Edl target Yan/Aop leads to a loss of heart cells irrespective of their subtype (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a description of the overexpression phenotype shown in Figure 5D.

claim: edl pnt double mutants mimic pnt mutants.
source: If the predominant function of Edl during CB specification is the inhibition of Pnt, edl pnt double mutants should mimic pnt mutants. In principle, this is what we observed (Figure 5E,F; quantifications in Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic epistasis experiment shown in Figure 5E, 5F, and 5I.

claim: edl aop double mutants show an additive combination of aop and edl single mutant phenotypes.
source: By contrast, edl aop double mutants show an additive combination of aop and edl single mutant phenotypes (compare Figure 5H with 5G and 4D; see also quantifications in Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a description of the genetic epistasis experiment shown in Figure 5G, 5H, and 5I.

claim: Amorphic aop mutants display a reduction in CB number irrespective of CB subtype.
source: Amorphic aop mutants display a reduction in CB number irrespective of CB subtype, which we ascribe to a permissive function during CB development that is probably linked to its well-documented role in restricting eve expression in the early dorsal mesoderm (Bidet et al., 2003; Halfon et al., 2000; Liu et al., 2006; Webber et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the aop mutant phenotype and an interpretation based on previous work.

claim: Manipulating aop activities does not lead to significant shifts in the oCBs:gCBs ratio.
source: Importantly, and in contrast to edl and pnt activity changes, manipulating aop activities does not lead to significant shifts in the oCBs:gCBs ratio (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the quantification shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Edl acts mainly via negative modulation of PntP2 activity during cardioblast diversification.
source: Thus, we suggest that Edl acts mainly via negative modulation of PntP2 activity during cardioblast diversification.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic epistasis experiments.

claim: The reduction in numbers of both svp-LacZ+ oCBs and OPCs at late stages in edl mutants suggests that edl affects the fates of their common progenitors.
source: The reduction in numbers of both svp-LacZ+ oCBs and OPCs at late stages (Figure 6D cf. 6C) suggests that edl already affects the fates of their common progenitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Mesodermal overexpression of edl leads to larger numbers of svp-LacZ+ cardiac cells, particularly of CBs.
source: Consistent with a function in promoting svp expression and oCBs fates, mesodermal overexpression of edl leads to larger numbers of svp-LacZ+ cardiac cells, particularly of CBs, where svp expression correlates with expanded Doc expression (Figure 6E,F).
evidence: This is a description of the overexpression phenotype shown in Figure 6E and 6F.

claim: svp expression can be suppressed by PntP2 hyperactivity.
source: As shown for Doc expression, svp expression can be suppressed by PntP2 hyperactivity (green asterisks in Figure 6H).
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype shown in Figure 6H.

claim: edl affects CB patterning by blocking Pnt activity upstream of svp.
source: These observations and further evaluation of the epistatic relations between svp and edl (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) demonstrate that edl affects CB patterning by blocking Pnt activity upstream of svp.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic epistasis experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: High levels of Pnt-GFP are present in the nuclei of gCB progenitors.
source: We confirmed and refined these observations showing that high levels of Pnt-GFP are present in the nuclei of gCB progenitors as identified by their position, characteristically enlarged size, presence of only low levels of Doc, and absence of svp-LacZ expression (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a description of the expression analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: PntP1-specific antibodies specifically label gCB progenitors.
source: We attribute these high total Pnt levels largely to a gCB-specific expression of the PntP1 isoform since PntP1-specific antibodies (Alvarez et al., 2003) specifically label gCB progenitors (Figure 7B), whereas pntP2 transcripts are present in a rather uniform pattern in the mesoderm including the cardiogenic area (Klämbt, 1993; and data not shown).
evidence: This is a description of the expression analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PntP1 is detected in an expanded pattern in the cardiogenic mesoderm of edl mutants.
source: First, we detect PntP1 in an expanded pattern in the cardiogenic mesoderm of edl mutants in which PntP2 activity is assumed to increase (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a description of the phenotype shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Overexpression of edl as well as genetic disruption of pntP2 resulted in a near-complete loss of cardiac PntP1.
source: Second, overexpression of edl (i.e. repression of PntP2 function) as well as genetic disruption of pntP2 resulted in a near-complete loss of cardiac PntP1 (Figure 7D,E; note persistent expression of PntP1 in other cells located more laterally).
evidence: This is a description of the phenotypes shown in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: The combined activities of Edl and PntP2 lead to the confined pntP1 expression in gCBs.
source: We conclude that the combined activities of Edl and PntP2 lead to the confined pntP1 expression in gCBs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the expression analysis of PntP1 in various genetic backgrounds.

claim: The EGF Spitz is a major, although not necessarily the sole factor for the MAPK-mediated activation of PntP2 in the context of gCB specification.
source: The EGF Spitz appears to be a major, although not necessarily the sole factor for the MAPK-mediated activation of PntP2 in this context, because PntP1 levels are reduced but not eradicated in cardiac cells of amorphic spi mutants (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of PntP1 expression in spi mutants shown in Figure 7F.

claim: mid is not required to directly promote tin expression in gCBs in absence of Svp.
source: This effect is also observed in mid1 svpAE127 double mutants, and there is no apparent loss of Tin in gCBs, demonstrating that mid is not required to directly promote tin expression in gCBs in absence of Svp.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of mid svp double mutants shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The expansion of svp-lacZ typical for mid mutants is attenuated in mid svp double mutants, suggesting a necessity of functional Svp for its own ectopic expression.
source: Notably, the expansion of svp-lacZ typical for mid mutants is attenuated in these double mutants, suggesting a necessity of functional Svp for its own ectopic expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of mid svp double mutants shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: An enhancer identified as a Tin target and named midE19 drives mid expression specifically in gCBs.
source: Notably, an enhancer identified as a Tin target and named midE19 (mid180 for a shorter minimal version) was recently shown to drive mid expression specifically in gCBs (Jin et al., 2013; Ryu et al., 2011; Figure 8A–C; Figure 9A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and data shown in Figure 8A-C and Figure 9A,C.

claim: Very little midE19-GFP activity is detectable in pnt mutants.
source: Consistent with our assumption that this enhancer is also a target of Pnt, very little midE19-GFP activity is detectable in pnt mutants (Figure 8D), reduced activity is observed in embryos with mesodermal edl overexpression (Figure 8E), and expanded activity is seen upon overexpression of PntP1 (Figure 8F; note occasional expansion into CBs with no detectable Tin) or PntP2VP16 (not shown).
evidence: This is a description of the reporter activity in various genetic backgrounds shown in Figure 8D-F.

claim: A reduction of midE19-driven GFP levels is observed in many of the retained Tin+ gCBs of rho mutants.
source: An observed reduction of midE19-driven GFP levels in many of the retained Tin+ gCBs of rho mutants (Figure 8G) corroborates that EGF signaling feeds into mid activation.
evidence: This is a description of the reporter activity in rho mutants shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Mutating a single ETS binding motif within the mid180 minimal cardiac enhancer leads to almost complete elimination of reporter activity.
source: The idea that mid is a target of Pnt is further supported by the almost complete elimination of reporter activity upon mutating a single ETS binding motif within the mid180 minimal cardiac enhancer (Figure 9A–D) as well as the strong reduction of endogenous mid transcription in emerging CBs during germ band retraction stages in pnt mutants (Figure 9E–H).
evidence: This is a description of the enhancer analysis shown in Figure 9A-D.

claim: Endogenous mid transcription is strongly reduced in emerging CBs during germ band retraction stages in pnt mutants.
source: The idea that mid is a target of Pnt is further supported by the almost complete elimination of reporter activity upon mutating a single ETS binding motif within the mid180 minimal cardiac enhancer (Figure 9A–D) as well as the strong reduction of endogenous mid transcription in emerging CBs during germ band retraction stages in pnt mutants (Figure 9E–H).
evidence: This is a description of the expression analysis shown in Figure 9E-H.

claim: After germ band retraction, endogenous mid is activated independently of pnt in all CBs.
source: After germ band retraction, endogenous mid is activated independently of pnt in all CBs (Figure 9J) as observed in the wild type (Figure 9I) indicating that distinct mechanisms regulate mid transcription in early gCB progenitors and maturing CBs.
evidence: This is a description of the expression analysis shown in Figure 9I and 9J.
